title: Arrested Twice in One Day.
description:
Submit a tip! Tips@Midwest-Safety.com

CONTACT US:
Complaints? Video submissions? Sponsorships? Collabs? Business inquires?

BE NICE:
The individuals presented in these videos may be suffering from the effects of alcohol, drug abuse, a mental health disorder or simply having a bad day. The videos should NOT be presumed to be representative of their general behavior. Everyone deserves to be treated with respect.

transcript.text: Going north and eight four, a little guy's pulling over and it's going to be a pursuit. And someone behind me calling up, please. Pursuit northbound 84, Adam Zero Paul, 834, 834, 3,4, a white Hyundai one occupant stolen vehicle. We got it to, we're heading northbound towards I-94, speeds are about 65 traffic flight right now. Pursuit of a stolen white Hyundai headed northbound on 84, cross-hunter, I-94, speeds are approximately, 60 to 65 right now. Go back southbound at Honey Creek. Try pit, pit, pit, pit, see what happens. Well, 70 miles an hour. We're not gonna go faster than that with that donut. All right, it just jumped into the parking lot at the store here. Lost control, crashed, the crash, it's back out on the road. Brookfield's gonna pit it. Parking lot right now is Brookfield's got right behind it. It's coming back out to 1-2-4. All right, it's up in the Aspen Dental parking lot right now. All right, lost the tire, lost the tire, pit, pit, pit, pit. Got him, I'm chasing that guy. He went across. All right, he's going in the Jimmy Johns right now. All right, I think we got the driver in custody right now that Jimmy John's lot in Brookfield. The car might have one more guy in it, not sure yet. I've got the driver in custody, taser deployed. Do you have scissors? That won't run next time, partner. Got anything on you? Any weapons or guns, drugs? Nothing. I got you. I got you. While officers may have the suspect in custody for now, after getting medical clearance At a nearby hospital, the suspect manages to do the unexpected. Here, stint up. I'll be taking off of me. My way, I'm 8-8 eastbound. This south of Lincoln, and by 87th place, I don't see him anymore. Over the next three hours, officers continue searching for the suspect with no luck. However, officers get their first lead when a report comes in of strange noises coming from someone's garage in the vicinity of the hospital. That's the shoes right there. There are shoes. Hey, shoes. You see them? Come out right now. This is the Westdale's Police Department. Come out now. Check it the dog? Yeah, go here, dog. He's in a car, garage here, give him to the police. 29, he's not in a custody. This suspect, Charles, was taken into custody a second time and promptly transported to jail. He was charged with criminal damage to property, second degree recklessly endangering safety, fleeing, eluding, escape, felony bail jumping, driving a v. vehicle without consent and resisting obstructing, with six of those charges being enhanced with a habitual criminality repeater modifier. Charles pled guilty to criminal damage to property, second degree recklessly endangering safety and fleeing eluding, with the rest of the charges being dismissed. He was ultimately sentenced to three years in the Wisconsin state prison system and two years of extended supervision. Control isn't lost in a fight, it's lost in one brief moment, and that moment normally doesn't look dramatic. It's the smallest motions, a hand on the door, a glance at the radio, just a half a second delay. That's all it takes because control doesn't get taken, it leaks, and fear does not wait for permission. Handcuffs never calm people down, they make them feel cornered and a corner person isn't thinking about charges or tomorrow. They just want air and freedom. That's exactly why cops keep their hands free because once attention splits between two things, control does have a clock on it. The crazy part is the cuff suspect running around doesn't reset anything. It forces officers to abandon containment and switch to recovery, which means wider searches, more force options and fewer chances to slow it back down. Custodies where professionalism gets tested the hardest, not by violence, but by routine, fatigue, and by thinking this part is easy. doesn't announce itself anymore it waits for comfort and the second comfort creeps in control is gone and what felt safe a moment ago suddenly isn't always remember handcuffs don't stop fear it traps it and trap fear doesn't negotiate it moves and it moves quickly
